<notes>
### tech-industry-updates/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-google-s-defense.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and Google's defense
Summary: Overview of the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, including CEO Sundar Pichai's testimony on default search engine deals, specific financial figures, and historical context regarding browser defaults.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable for consumers.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults was made with the consumer in mind to gather data and be the best search engine across devices. On October 28, Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of this total went directly to Apple, per a New York Times report. Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.

Historical context includes a 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showing that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. In 2018, Pichai admitted attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device to create inseparable services, but Cook refused as Apple does not preload third-party software. Additionally, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours; Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold.
</notes>

### tech-industry-updates/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the start of SBF's fraud trial, the founding of FTX and Alameda, the 2022 collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, SBF's arrest and extradition, and the guilty pleas of other executives.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing for Chapter 11 in January.

### tech-industry-updates/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Details the prosecution and defense opening statements in the SBF trial, including key allegations, the defense's characterization of SBF, and the testimony of early witnesses like Marc-Antoine Julliard and Adam Yedidia.

The trial against former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, alleged that SBF stole billions from thousands of victims and lied to the world. They detailed a scheme involving Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison to gain secret access to customer funds, with actions including directing employees to conceal money flows and forging financial documents. The prosecution characterized SBF as a 'man' who built a thriving exchange, traveled internationally, and financed risky bets, claiming all his public appearances were built on lies.

In contrast, defense attorney Mark Cohen presented SBF as a well-meaning startup founder who acted in 'good faith,' arguing he did not defraud anyone. Cohen noted SBF's appearance, which showed more prominent cheekbones after spending seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and aimed to present him as anything but the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain.' SBF himself described Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He argued Alameda acted legally as a customer, payment processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' SBF blamed Ellison for not adequately protecting the hedge fund from market risks and claimed he offered to give up personal wealth when the crisis approached, concluding he built two billion-dollar businesses without stealing money.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified that he attempted to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8, 2021, but never succeeded. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of SBF, testified that he had legal immunity and persuaded SBF to join him as a trader at Alameda and developer at FTX after SBF left Jane Street, citing concern that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime. The court adjourned at 4:30 p.m., with Yedidia scheduled to continue testimony on Thursday, followed by Matt Huang and Gary Wang.
</notes>

### tech-industry-updates/apple-defends-google-search-deal-in-court-there-wasn-t-a.md

Title: Apple defends Google Search deal in court: 'There wasn't a valid alternative'
Summary: Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google that Apple had no valid alternative to Google's search engine, negotiated the 2016 ISA with Sundar Pichai, and argued the deal prioritized user experience over economics.

Eddy Cue testified in the US v. Google antitrust trial defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA), which has made Google the default search engine on Apple devices since 2002. In 2016, Cue negotiated the current iteration of the ISA with Google CEO Sundar Pichai; while Apple sought a higher revenue share and Pichai wanted to maintain the status quo, they compromised on an undisclosed percentage.

Cue argued there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and none exists now, stating Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. He emphasized that the deal was about more than economics. Regarding user experience, Cue acknowledged the ISA did not allow Apple to offer search engine choices during setup, citing speed and user experience as reasons for defaulting to Google.

On privacy, Cue agreed Apple values user privacy and claimed Apple offers better privacy than Google, citing ISA provisions for login-free searches and anti-tracking measures. When questioned about the ISA's impact on Apple's profits, Bellshaw asked if it represented a significant portion; Cue replied that Apple does not view it that way because the platform's overall appeal makes the agreement successful. Schmidtlein led Cue through Safari's history, noting Google integration was a user interface innovation mentioned in pre-2003 promotional materials. Cue explained that before 2003, users had to type specific URLs to search, whereas Apple's system redirects non-URL text to search. Schmidtlein and Cue argued that Google helped Safari succeed as a great product and that switching search engines is easy, referencing Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing. Finally, in response to DOJ questions about whether Google is the best search engine or simply pays the most, and what the market looks like without those payments, Cue stated Apple never considered these factors.
</notes>

Question: After the 'Fortune' article on October 4, 2023, discussing Sam Bankman-Fried's actions and the state of FTX, and the 'TechCrunch' article mentioning the prosecution's allegations against Sam Bankman-Fried, is there consistency in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's legal situation according to these sources?

<notes>
### tech-industry-updates/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Details the prosecution and defense opening statements in the SBF trial, including key allegations, the defense's characterization of SBF, and the testimony of early witnesses like Marc-Antoine Julliard and Adam Yedidia.

The trial against former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, alleged that SBF stole billions from thousands of victims and lied to the world. They detailed a scheme involving Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison to gain secret access to customer funds, with actions including directing employees to conceal money flows and forging financial documents. The prosecution characterized SBF as a 'man' who built a thriving exchange, traveled internationally, and financed risky bets, claiming all his public appearances were built on lies.

In contrast, defense attorney Mark Cohen presented SBF as a well-meaning startup founder who acted in 'good faith,' arguing he did not defraud anyone. Cohen noted SBF's appearance, which showed more prominent cheekbones after spending seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and aimed to present him as anything but the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain.' SBF himself described Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He argued Alameda acted legally as a customer, payment processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' SBF blamed Ellison for not adequately protecting the hedge fund from market risks and claimed he offered to give up personal wealth when the crisis approached, concluding he built two billion-dollar businesses without stealing money.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified that he attempted to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8, 2021, but never succeeded. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of SBF, testified that he had legal immunity and persuaded SBF to join him as a trader at Alameda and developer at FTX after SBF left Jane Street, citing concern that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime. The court adjourned at 4:30 p.m., with Yedidia scheduled to continue testimony on Thursday, followed by Matt Huang and Gary Wang.

### tech-industry-updates/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the start of SBF's fraud trial, the founding of FTX and Alameda, the 2022 collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, SBF's arrest and extradition, and the guilty pleas of other executives.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing for Chapter 11 in January.
</notes>

### tech-industry-updates/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Details the prosecution and defense opening statements in the SBF trial, including key allegations, the defense's characterization of SBF, and the testimony of early witnesses like Marc-Antoine Julliard and Adam Yedidia.

The trial against former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, alleged that SBF stole billions from thousands of victims and lied to the world. They detailed a scheme involving Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison to gain secret access to customer funds, with actions including directing employees to conceal money flows and forging financial documents. The prosecution characterized SBF as a 'man' who built a thriving exchange, traveled internationally, and financed risky bets, claiming all his public appearances were built on lies.

In contrast, defense attorney Mark Cohen presented SBF as a well-meaning startup founder who acted in 'good faith,' arguing he did not defraud anyone. Cohen noted SBF's appearance, which showed more prominent cheekbones after spending seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and aimed to present him as anything but the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain.' SBF himself described Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He argued Alameda acted legally as a customer, payment processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' SBF blamed Ellison for not adequately protecting the hedge fund from market risks and claimed he offered to give up personal wealth when the crisis approached, concluding he built two billion-dollar businesses without stealing money.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified that he attempted to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8, 2021, but never succeeded. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of SBF, testified that he had legal immunity and persuaded SBF to join him as a trader at Alameda and developer at FTX after SBF left Jane Street, citing concern that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime. The court adjourned at 4:30 p.m., with Yedidia scheduled to continue testimony on Thursday, followed by Matt Huang and Gary Wang.

### tech-industry-updates/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-to-cancel-presidential-bid-and-ftx.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump to cancel presidential bid and FTX collapse
Summary: SBF offered $5 billion to Donald Trump to cancel his 2024 re-run; he was accused of orchestrating FTX's collapse, raised $2B from major VCs, and faced criticism for his management style and financial dealings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) is the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF pleaded not-guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in Manhattan Federal Court. He reportedly offered $5 billion to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential re-run bid, though he also looked to back candidates on the Democratic side of the aisle and met with Mitch McConnell to discuss funding Republican candidates to offset Trump's influence.

SBF raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers that included Sequoia, Temasek, Tiger Global, and dozens more. Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial; Lewis was introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, asked to meet SBF in Berkeley to 'evaluate his character,' and met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30, and 60 Minutes got involved with the story, shooting a segment with SBF and Lewis.

FTX's trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. To lend legitimacy, Tom Brady was paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million for marketing deals. Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. SBF's eyes moved back and forth during a TV appearance while trying to win a video game simultaneously.

The hard crash occurred as FTX cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF is denied bail, blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda/FTX, and accused of causing a ripple effect of crypto woes. Ayelet Noff, CEO of Sliced Brand, states SBF lacked management experience, was over his head, and delayed crypto adoption by at least one to two years. Michael Lewis's interview with SBF is criticized for defending him as an 'effective altruist' and claiming FTX had a great real business, despite no proof of idealism. FTX failure resulted from financial discrepancies between the exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, a trader on the platform.
</notes>

Title: Google Search dominance, data practices, and competitive challenges
Summary: An analysis of Google's market dominance, data collection scope, personalization capabilities, and the controversies surrounding its search manipulation and default status.

Google Search faces scrutiny regarding its market dominance, data collection practices, and the fairness of its default status. Kent Walker argues Google is preferred because it is the best, not just the default, citing user choice in Mozilla and Windows scenarios. However, users frequently revert to Google after Mozilla set Yahoo as Firefox default and after Microsoft set Bing as default in 2021, indicating displacement friction.

Google collects user searches, smart speaker interactions, clicked results, and ads, favoring DuckDuckGo for privacy despite potential performance issues. Its index is over 100 million gigabytes, using machine learning to rank results by quality and usability. In 2022, Google ran almost 900,000 quality tests with independent raters. Critics like Megan Grey contend that semantic keyword matching reduces precision to widen content pools and increase ad auctions. Megan Grey, former DuckDuckGo VP, admits possible evidence misinterpretation but maintains Google manipulates Search to maximize ad revenue.

Danny Sullivan states that ad systems do not affect organic results (blue links); keyword matching connects people to ads, while a separate process matches organic results to queries using meaning matching. Conversely, Bing Chat failed to filter results for 'kids BMX bike green' under $200, returning only options over $300, and lacks functional follow-up questions despite an overhaul with generative AI. Global data creation grew from 9 ZB/year in 2013 to 120 ZB in 2023, shifting from static websites to live information nested in apps. The US faces an uphill battle proving Google broke the law to achieve its market status quo, while others gain insight into Google's market share usage. Wired removed an article on Google Search manipulation, though social sharing and coverage elsewhere show public willingness to accept foul play and suspicion of privacy invasion.

Summary: Overview of the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, including CEO Sundar Pichai's testimony on default search engine deals, specific financial figures, and historical context regarding browser defaults.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable for consumers.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults was made with the consumer in mind to gather data and be the best search engine across devices. On October 28, Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of this total went directly to Apple, per a New York Times report. Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.

Historical context includes a 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showing that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. In 2018, Pichai admitted attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device to create inseparable services, but Cook refused as Apple does not preload third-party software. Additionally, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours; Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold.
</notes>

Title: Apple defends Google Search deal in court: 'There wasn't a valid alternative'
Summary: Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google that Apple had no valid alternative to Google's search engine, negotiated the 2016 ISA with Sundar Pichai, and argued the deal prioritized user experience over economics.

Eddy Cue testified in the US v. Google antitrust trial defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA), which has made Google the default search engine on Apple devices since 2002. In 2016, Cue negotiated the current iteration of the ISA with Google CEO Sundar Pichai; while Apple sought a higher revenue share and Pichai wanted to maintain the status quo, they compromised on an undisclosed percentage.

Cue argued there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and none exists now, stating Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. He emphasized that the deal was about more than economics. Regarding user experience, Cue acknowledged the ISA did not allow Apple to offer search engine choices during setup, citing speed and user experience as reasons for defaulting to Google.

On privacy, Cue agreed Apple values user privacy and claimed Apple offers better privacy than Google, citing ISA provisions for login-free searches and anti-tracking measures. When questioned about the ISA's impact on Apple's profits, Bellshaw asked if it represented a significant portion; Cue replied that Apple does not view it that way because the platform's overall appeal makes the agreement successful. Schmidtlein led Cue through Safari's history, noting Google integration was a user interface innovation mentioned in pre-2003 promotional materials. Cue explained that before 2003, users had to type specific URLs to search, whereas Apple's system redirects non-URL text to search. Schmidtlein and Cue argued that Google helped Safari succeed as a great product and that switching search engines is easy, referencing Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing. Finally, in response to DOJ questions about whether Google is the best search engine or simply pays the most, and what the market looks like without those payments, Cue stated Apple never considered these factors.

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI technologies like Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, and older tools like the Knowledge Graph launched in May 2012.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, invoking the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. The suit alleges that Google and Alphabet engage in anticompetitive behavior by siphoning off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI technologies such as Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, as well as older tools like the Knowledge Graph, which was launched in May 2012.

The Knowledge Graph grew to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities by 2020. The lawsuit alleges Google compiled this database by extracting information from publishers' websites and open source/licensed databases, misappropriating content that 'starves the free press' and costs publishers billions of dollars. A Wall Street Journal report cited by the suit states that when The Atlantic modeled Google integrating AI into search, 75% of the time AI would answer queries without a click-through to the publisher's site. Since Google drives nearly 40% of publisher traffic, publishers expect to lose 20-40% of their website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out.

The case cites concerns over changing AdSense rates and Google's destruction of chat messages, referencing the recent Epic Games antitrust lawsuit where Epic won. The suit seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products (including rivals' AI) and allowing opt-out publishers to appear in search results. Plus cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news, magazine, and digital publications, noting news sites were the third-largest category of AI training data.

The U.S. lawsuit follows a Google agreement with the Canadian government to pay $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) annually to Canadian news organizations based on headcount, while negotiations with Meta remain unresolved. Meta began blocking news in Canada in August due to pressure from the new Canadian law to pay for content. The case arrives alongside the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, referencing a 2020 DOJ civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising. Hausfeld law firm states Google's anticompetitive scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press.

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Details the prosecution and defense opening statements in the SBF trial, including key allegations, the defense's characterization of SBF, and the testimony of early witnesses like Marc-Antoine Julliard and Adam Yedidia.

The trial against former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, alleged that SBF stole billions from thousands of victims and lied to the world. They detailed a scheme involving Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison to gain secret access to customer funds, with actions including directing employees to conceal money flows and forging financial documents. The prosecution characterized SBF as a 'man' who built a thriving exchange, traveled internationally, and financed risky bets, claiming all his public appearances were built on lies.

In contrast, defense attorney Mark Cohen presented SBF as a well-meaning startup founder who acted in 'good faith,' arguing he did not defraud anyone. Cohen noted SBF's appearance, which showed more prominent cheekbones after spending seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and aimed to present him as anything but the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain.' SBF himself described Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He argued Alameda acted legally as a customer, payment processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' SBF blamed Ellison for not adequately protecting the hedge fund from market risks and claimed he offered to give up personal wealth when the crisis approached, concluding he built two billion-dollar businesses without stealing money.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified that he attempted to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8, 2021, but never succeeded. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of SBF, testified that he had legal immunity and persuaded SBF to join him as a trader at Alameda and developer at FTX after SBF left Jane Street, citing concern that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime. The court adjourned at 4:30 p.m., with Yedidia scheduled to continue testimony on Thursday, followed by Matt Huang and Gary Wang.
</notes>
